tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Drag on smooth circular cylinders towed through the tank. 1in, 2in and

This is a [Calkit](https://calkit.org) project. Everything from raw data to

   logged temperature), uncertainties -> `processed/cd.csv`,
   `results/summary.json`, and the LaTeX macros/tables used by the paper.
3. `plot-*` (`scripts/plot_*.py`): figures in `figures/*.pdf`.

   Docker, so Docker must be running).

"""Shared constants and helpers for the tow tank drag analysis."""

import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

G = 9.81  # m/s^2
L_SUB = 0.60  # submerged cylinder length, m
TANK_WIDTH = 0.90  # m
TANK_DEPTH = 0.75  # m

# Sampling windows (s) used for every run
TARE_WINDOW = (0.0, 1.0)  # carriage at rest before the tow
STEADY_WINDOW = (3.0, 8.0)  # constant-speed portion of the tow
POST_WINDOW_LENGTH = 1.0  # last second of the record, carriage at rest again

# Each raw-data batch, the DAQ file format it was written in, and the
# load cell calibration in force when it was acquired
BATCHES = {
    "2025-10-14": {"format": "v1", "calibration": "loadcell_2025-09.csv"},
    "2025-11-03": {"format": "v1", "calibration": "loadcell_2025-09.csv"},
    "2026-03-12": {"format": "v2", "calibration": "loadcell_2026-03.csv"},
}

# A post-run zero shift larger than this (N) marks a run as drifted
ZERO_SHIFT_TOL = 0.05


def read_run(path: str, fmt: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a raw run file into a frame with columns ``t`` (s) and ``V``."""
    if fmt == "v1":
        d = pd.read_csv(path, comment="#")
    elif fmt == "v2":
        # DAQ software update in March 2026: semicolon separated, short names
        d = pd.read_csv(path, sep=";")
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown format {fmt}")
    d.columns = ["t", "V"]
    return d


def fit_calibration(path: str) -> dict:
    """Linear fit of load cell voltage vs. applied force.

    Returns sensitivity (V/N), offset (V), standard error of the sensitivity,
    and the max residual expressed in N.
    """
    cal = pd.read_csv(path)
    force = cal.mass_g / 1000 * G
    p, cov = np.polyfit(force, cal.voltage_V, 1, cov=True)
    resid = cal.voltage_V - np.polyval(p, force)
    return {
        "sens": p[0],
        "offset": p[1],
        "sens_se": np.sqrt(cov[0, 0]),
        "max_resid_N": np.abs(resid).max() / p[0],
        "max_load_N": force.max(),
    }


def run_number(path: str) -> int:
    return int(os.path.basename(path)[4:7])


def water_density(temp_c):
    """Density of air-free water in kg/m^3 (Kell, 1975)."""
    t = np.asarray(temp_c, dtype=float)
    num = (
        999.83952
        + 16.945176 * t
        - 7.9870401e-3 * t**2
        - 46.170461e-6 * t**3
        + 105.56302e-9 * t**4
        - 280.54253e-12 * t**5
    )
    return num / (1 + 16.879850e-3 * t)


def water_viscosity(temp_c):
    """Dynamic viscosity of water in Pa s (Kestin et al., 1978), 0-40 C."""
    t = np.asarray(temp_c, dtype=float)
    dt = 20 - t
    log_ratio = dt / (t + 96) * (1.2364 - 1.37e-3 * dt + 5.7e-6 * dt**2)
    return 1.002e-3 * 10**log_ratio
"""Compute drag coefficient and Reynolds number for every run.

Water properties are evaluated at the temperature logged for each run.
Writes the per-run table, a JSON summary, and LaTeX macros/tables used by
the paper so that every number quoted in the text comes from this script.
"""

import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import towtank as tt

ST = 0.2  # nominal Strouhal number, only used to count shedding cycles

forces = pd.read_csv("processed/forces.csv")
log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")
cals = json.load(open("processed/calibrations.json"))
df = forces.merge(log, left_on="run", right_on="run_id", validate="1:1")

D = df.diameter_mm / 1000
U = df.speed_m_s
df["rho"] = tt.water_density(df.water_temp_c)
df["nu"] = tt.water_viscosity(df.water_temp_c) / df.rho
df["Re"] = U * D / df.nu
df["Re_20C"] = U * D / 1.004e-6  # as in the original notebook, for comparison
df["Fr_D"] = U / np.sqrt(tt.G * D)
df["aspect_ratio"] = tt.L_SUB / D
df["blockage"] = D * tt.L_SUB / (tt.TANK_WIDTH * tt.TANK_DEPTH)
q_area = 0.5 * df.rho * U**2 * D * tt.L_SUB
df["Cd"] = df.F_mean / q_area
df["Cd_drift_corr"] = df.F_mean_drift_corr / q_area
# Simple continuity estimate of solid blockage: velocity past the cylinder
# raised by 1 / (1 - S/C). Reported as a sensitivity check only.
df["Cd_cont"] = df.Cd * (1 - df.blockage) ** 2

# Force uncertainty for the mean (standard uncertainty, N): calibration
# residual combined with the standard error of the mean over the steady
# window, taking one independent sample per shedding cycle
window = tt.STEADY_WINDOW[1] - tt.STEADY_WINDOW[0]
n_cycles = ST * U * window / D
cal_resid = df.calibration.map(lambda c: cals[c]["max_resid_N"])
sens_rel = df.calibration.map(lambda c: cals[c]["sens_se"] / cals[c]["sens"])
u_F = np.sqrt(
    cal_resid**2 + (df.F_std / np.sqrt(n_cycles)) ** 2 + (sens_rel * df.F_mean) ** 2
)
df["n_cycles"] = n_cycles
df["u_F"] = u_F
df["u_Cd"] = df.Cd * u_F / df.F_mean
df["max_cal_load_N"] = df.calibration.map(lambda c: cals[c]["max_load_N"])
df["above_cal_range"] = df.F_mean > df.max_cal_load_N
df["used"] = ~df.drifted

cols = [
    "run", "date", "cylinder", "diameter_mm", "speed_m_s", "water_temp_c",
    "rho", "nu", "Re", "Re_20C", "Fr_D", "aspect_ratio", "blockage",
    "F_mean", "F_std", "u_F", "Cd", "u_Cd", "Cd_drift_corr", "Cd_cont",
    "n_cycles", "zero_shift_N", "drifted", "above_cal_range", "used",
]
df = df[cols].sort_values(["diameter_mm", "run"])
df.to_csv("processed/cd.csv", index=False)

# ---- Summary statistics ----
ok = df[df.used]
order = ["1in", "1.5in", "2in"]
per_cyl = {}
for cyl in order:
    g = ok[ok.cylinder == cyl]
    per_cyl[cyl] = {
        "D_mm": float(g.diameter_mm.iloc[0]),
        "n": int(len(g)),
        "Cd_mean": float(g.Cd.mean()),
        "Cd_std": float(g.Cd.std()),
        "Cd_min": float(g.Cd.min()),
        "Cd_max": float(g.Cd.max()),
        "Cd_cont_mean": float(g.Cd_cont.mean()),
        "Re_min": float(g.Re.min()),
        "Re_max": float(g.Re.max()),
        "Fr_max": float(g.Fr_D.max()),
        "T_min": float(g.water_temp_c.min()),
        "T_max": float(g.water_temp_c.max()),
        "aspect_ratio": float(g.aspect_ratio.iloc[0]),
        "blockage": float(g.blockage.iloc[0]),
    }
# Linear trend of Cd with log10(Re), all usable runs
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(np.log10(ok.Re), ok.Cd, 1)
r17 = df[df.run == 17].iloc[0]
summary = {
    "n_runs": int(len(df)),
    "n_used": int(len(ok)),
    "excluded_runs": df.run[~df.used].tolist(),
    "Cd_mean_all": float(ok.Cd.mean()),
    "Cd_std_all": float(ok.Cd.std()),
    "Cd_trend_per_decade": float(slope),
    "Re_min": float(ok.Re.min()),
    "Re_max": float(ok.Re.max()),
    "Re_ratio_20C_max": float((df.Re_20C / df.Re).max()),
    "Re_ratio_20C_min": float((df.Re_20C / df.Re).min()),
    "u_Cd_rel_min": float((ok.u_Cd / ok.Cd).min()),
    "u_Cd_rel_max": float((ok.u_Cd / ok.Cd).max()),
    "u_Cd_rel_median": float((ok.u_Cd / ok.Cd).median()),
    "run17_Cd": float(r17.Cd),
    "run17_Cd_drift_corr": float(r17.Cd_drift_corr),

    "F_max": float(df.F_mean.max()),

}

with open("results/summary.json", "w") as fp:
    json.dump(summary, fp, indent=2)

# ---- LaTeX macros ----
os.makedirs("results", exist_ok=True)

    "NRuns": f"{len(df)}",
    "NUsed": f"{len(ok)}",

TANK_DEPTH = 0.75  # m

TARE_WINDOW = (0.0, 1.0)  # carriage at rest before the tow
STEADY_WINDOW = (3.0, 8.0)  # constant-speed portion of the tow
POST_WINDOW_LENGTH = 1.0  # last second of the record, carriage at rest again

# Each raw-data batch, the DAQ file format it was written in, and the
# load cell calibration in force when it was acquired
BATCHES = {
    "2025-10-14": {"format": "v1", "calibration": "loadcell_2025-09.csv"},
    "2025-11-03": {"format": "v1", "calibration": "loadcell_2025-09.csv"},
    "2026-03-12": {"format": "v2", "calibration": "loadcell_2026-03.csv"},
}

# A post-run zero shift larger than this (N) marks a run as drifted
ZERO_SHIFT_TOL = 0.05


def read_run(path: str, fmt: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a raw run file into a frame with columns ``t`` (s) and ``V``."""
    if fmt == "v1":
        d = pd.read_csv(path, comment="#")
    elif fmt == "v2":
        # DAQ software update in March 2026: semicolon separated, short names
        d = pd.read_csv(path, sep=";")
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown format {fmt}")
    d.columns = ["t", "V"]
    return d


def fit_calibration(path: str) -> dict:
    """Linear fit of load cell voltage vs. applied force.

    Returns sensitivity (V/N), offset (V), standard error of the sensitivity,
    and the max residual expressed in N.
    """
    cal = pd.read_csv(path)
    force = cal.mass_g / 1000 * G
    p, cov = np.polyfit(force, cal.voltage_V, 1, cov=True)
    resid = cal.voltage_V - np.polyval(p, force)
    return {
        "sens": p[0],
        "offset": p[1],
        "sens_se": np.sqrt(cov[0, 0]),
        "max_resid_N": np.abs(resid).max() / p[0],
        "max_load_N": force.max(),
    }

    return int(os.path.basename(path)[4:7])

    """Density of air-free water in kg/m^3 (Kell, 1975)."""
    t = np.asarray(temp_c, dtype=float)
    num = (

        - 7.9870401e-3 * t**2
        - 46.170461e-6 * t**3
        + 105.56302e-9 * t**4

    return 1.002e-3 * 10**log_ratio

    27	\begin{abstract}
    28	We report mean drag measurements on three smooth circular cylinders
    29	(diameters 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8~mm) towed vertically through a water tank
    30	at speeds of 0.2--1.1~m/s, with a submerged length of 0.6~m.
    31	Using water properties evaluated at the measured temperature of each run,
    32	the experiments span $Re = \ReMin$--$\ReMax$.

    34	for load cell drift.

    36	diameter over this range, with an overall mean of
    37	$C_D = \CdMeanAll \pm \CdStdAll$ (mean $\pm$ standard deviation), and
    38	per-cylinder means of \CdMeanOne, \CdMeanOneHalf{} and \CdMeanTwo.

    42	aspect ratio ($L/D = 12$--24) and the free surface, which this test matrix
    43	does not separate, and we describe a data reduction procedure that is fully
    44	reproducible from the raw load cell records.

    50	\section{Introduction}
    51	\label{sec:intro}
    52	
    53	The mean drag of a circular cylinder in cross-flow is among the most
    54	thoroughly documented quantities in fluid mechanics
    55	\citep{Roshko1961,Zdravkovich1997,Williamson1996}.
    56	In the subcritical regime, $10^3 \lesssim Re \lesssim 2\times10^5$, the
    57	boundary layer separates laminar, the wake is dominated by periodic vortex
    58	shedding, and the drag coefficient of a nominally two-dimensional cylinder is
    59	roughly constant at $C_D \approx 1.0$--1.2
    60	\todo{cite specific reference data and the value you want to compare
    61	against}.
    62	
    63	Laboratory measurements rarely reproduce the two-dimensional ideal.
    64	Finite span, end conditions, blockage by the facility walls and, for
    65	surface-piercing models, the free surface all modify the measured drag
    66	\citep{WestApelt1982,ChaplinTeigen2003}.
    67	Tow tanks are attractive for such measurements because the free-stream is
    68	quiescent and its velocity is set by the carriage, but the model typically
    69	pierces the free surface and spans only part of the water depth.
    70	
    71	\todo{Motivation: why these measurements? E.g., facility validation, a
    72	teaching lab benchmark, a baseline for a later study. State the contribution
    73	clearly here.}
    74	In this paper we report drag measurements on three cylinders over a
    75	tenfold range of Reynolds number, describe the calibration and data
    76	reduction in detail, and assess the main sources of bias.
    77	
    78	%-----------------------------------------------------------------------
    79	\section{Experimental setup}
    80	\label{sec:setup}
    81	
    82	\subsection{Facility and models}
    83	
    84	Experiments were performed in a tow tank of cross-section
    85	0.90~m (width) $\times$ 0.75~m (water depth)
    86	\todo{facility name, location, tank length, carriage drive and speed
    87	control; how carriage speed was verified}.
    88	Three smooth circular cylinders of diameter $D = 25.4$, 38.1 and
    89	50.8~mm (1, 1.5 and 2~in) were mounted vertically from the carriage with a
    90	submerged length of $L = 0.60$~m, giving aspect ratios $L/D$ of
    91	\AROne, \AROneHalf{} and \ARTwo{} (table~\ref{tab:cylinders}).
    92	\todo{Cylinder material and surface finish; mounting arrangement; is the
    93	lower end free (0.15~m gap to the tank floor) or fitted with an end plate?
    94	Is any part of the support strut wetted?}
    95	
    96	\subsection{Force measurement and calibration}
    97	
    98	The streamwise force on the model was measured with a single-axis load cell
    99	\todo{make/model, rated capacity, mounting} sampled at 200~Hz.
   100	The load cell was calibrated in situ by hanging known masses of
   101	0--2000~g (0--\CalMaxLoad~N), loading and then unloading, and fitting a
   102	straight line to output voltage versus applied force
   103	(figure~\ref{fig:calibration}).
   104	The September 2025 calibration, which applies to the October and November
   105	2025 tests, gave a sensitivity of \CalOneSens~mV/N.
   106	The load cell was remounted before the March 2026 tests and recalibrated,
   107	giving \CalTwoSens~mV/N, a change of \SensChange\%.
   108	The largest residual from either fit corresponds to
   109	\CalOneResid--\CalTwoResid~mN, and the loading and unloading points agree
   110	to within the same amount, so hysteresis is negligible.
   111	The March 2026 data were recorded with an updated version of the
   112	acquisition software, which changed only the file format.
   113	
   114	\begin{figure}
   115	  \centering
   116	  \includegraphics{calibration.pdf}
   117	  \caption{Load cell calibrations before (Sep.\ 2025) and after
   118	  (Mar.\ 2026) the load cell was remounted. Lines are least-squares fits;
   119	  legend values are the fitted sensitivities.}
   120	  \label{fig:calibration}
   121	\end{figure}
   122	
   123	\subsection{Test matrix and procedure}
   124	
   125	Each cylinder was towed at ten nominal speeds, $U = 0.2$--1.1~m/s in
   126	0.1~m/s steps, giving \NRuns{} runs in total (appendix~\ref{app:runs}).
   127	The 25.4~mm cylinder was tested on 14 October 2025, the 50.8~mm cylinder on
   128	3 November 2025 and the 38.1~mm cylinder on 12 March 2026.
   129	Water temperature was recorded for every run and ranged from 13.7 to
   130	17.6\,$^\circ$C across the three campaigns.
   131	Each record is 12~s long: the carriage is at rest for the first second,
   132	accelerates to constant speed, decelerates at about $t = 9$~s and is at
   133	rest again for the final second (figure~\ref{fig:timeseries}a).
   134	\todo{Waiting time between runs; how residual motion in the tank was
   135	handled (the run log notes a small wave from the previous run before run
   136	4).}

   139	\section{Data reduction}
   140	\label{sec:reduction}
   141	
   142	\subsection{Mean drag force}
   143	
   144	For each run, the zero (tare) voltage is the mean over the first second,
   145	while the carriage is at rest. The force signal is
   146	$F(t) = [V(t) - V_\mathrm{tare}]/S$, where $S$ is the calibration
   147	sensitivity in force for that campaign, and the mean drag
   148	$\overline{F}$ is the average of $F(t)$ over the constant-speed window
   149	$3 < t < 8$~s (figure~\ref{fig:timeseries}a).
   150	The window starts after the start-up transient has decayed and ends before
   151	the carriage decelerates; it contains between about 4 and 43 vortex shedding
   152	cycles, depending on speed and diameter, assuming a Strouhal number of 0.2.
   153	\todo{Confirm the window against the carriage speed record if
   154	available.}
   155	
   156	\begin{figure}
   157	  \centering
   158	  \includegraphics{timeseries.pdf}
   159	  \caption{Load cell force records. (a) A typical run: shading marks the tare
   160	  window and the averaging window, and the black line is $\overline{F}$.
   161	  (b) Run~17, in which the signal drifts upward through the tow and does not
   162	  return to zero once the carriage stops; this run is excluded.}
   163	  \label{fig:timeseries}
   164	\end{figure}
   165	
   166	\subsection{Drag coefficient and Reynolds number}
   167	
   168	The drag coefficient and Reynolds number are
   169	\begin{equation}
   170	  C_D = \frac{\overline{F}}{\tfrac12 \rho U^2 D L},
   171	  \qquad
   172	  Re = \frac{U D}{\nu},
   173	\end{equation}
   174	where $U$ is the nominal carriage speed and $L$ is the submerged length.
   175	The density $\rho$ and kinematic viscosity $\nu$ are evaluated at the water
   176	temperature recorded for each run, using the correlations of
   177	\citet{Kell1975} and \citet{Kestin1978}.
   178	Water temperatures in these tests were 3--6\,$^\circ$C below 20\,$^\circ$C,
   179	so using the 20\,$^\circ$C viscosity would have overestimated $Re$ by
   180	\ReBiasMin--\ReBiasMax\%.
   181	We also report the diameter-based Froude number
   182	$Fr_D = U/\sqrt{gD}$, which ranges from \FrMin{} to \FrMax.
   183	
   184	\subsection{Data quality checks}
   185	\label{sec:quality}
   186	
   187	As a check on zero drift, the mean signal over the final second of each
   188	record, when the carriage is again at rest, is compared with the tare.
   189	For 29 of the 30 runs, this post-run zero shift is below 5~mN.
   190	For run~17 (50.8~mm cylinder, 0.8~m/s) the shift is \RunSeventeenShift~N,
   191	and the signal increases steadily throughout the tow
   192	(figure~\ref{fig:timeseries}b). This agrees with the experimenter's note
   193	at the time. Run~17 is therefore excluded. Its uncorrected drag
   194	coefficient is \RunSeventeenCd. If the zero is instead assumed to drift
   195	linearly between the pre- and post-run rest periods, $C_D$ becomes
   196	\RunSeventeenCdCorr, which agrees with the neighbouring runs. This suggests
   197	that the anomaly is instrumental, but we do not use the corrected value.
   198	\todo{Repeat run 17 if the cylinder can be re-tested; identify cause of
   199	drift (e.g.\ thermal, cable, mount slip).}
   200	
   201	The mean force in run~20 (\FMax~N) slightly exceeds the largest
   202	calibration load (\CalMaxLoad~N). Given the linearity of the calibration,
   203	we retain this run, but note that it relies on a small extrapolation.
   204	
   205	\subsection{Uncertainty}
   206	
   207	The standard uncertainty of $\overline{F}$ combines three contributions
   208	in quadrature:
   209	(i) the largest calibration residual, as a conservative bound on
   210	non-linearity and zero error;
   211	(ii) the standard error of the sensitivity fit; and
   212	(iii) the standard error of the mean over the averaging window, which
   213	treats each shedding cycle as one independent sample.
   214	The resulting standard uncertainty in $C_D$ is \UCdMin--\UCdMax\%
   215	(median \UCdMedian\%). The largest values occur at the lowest speeds,
   216	where the mean force is only a few tenths of a newton and the calibration
   217	residual dominates.
   218	These estimates exclude uncertainties in carriage speed, diameter and
   219	submerged length; a 1\% error in $U$ alone would contribute 2\% to $C_D$.
   220	\todo{Add carriage speed, $D$ and $L$ uncertainties (meniscus/waterline,
   221	free-surface set-down at higher speeds) and update the budget.}
   222	There are no repeat runs at the same condition, so run-to-run repeatability
   223	can only be inferred from the scatter of $C_D$ about its mean, which is
   224	$\pm\CdStdAll$ (one standard deviation).
   225	
   226	%-----------------------------------------------------------------------
   227	\section{Results}
   228	\label{sec:results}
   229	
   230	Figure~\ref{fig:cd} shows $C_D$ against $Re$ for all three cylinders, and
   231	table~\ref{tab:cylinders} summarises each data set.
   232	Over the full range $Re = \ReMin$--$\ReMax$, the drag coefficient lies
   233	between about 1.09 and 1.22, with an overall mean of
   234	$\CdMeanAll \pm \CdStdAll$.
   235	The per-cylinder means are \CdMeanOne{} ($D = 25.4$~mm),
   236	\CdMeanOneHalf{} (38.1~mm) and \CdMeanTwo{} (50.8~mm). These differ by
   237	less than the scatter within each set, so diameter has no resolvable
   238	effect.
   239	In the regions where the cylinders overlap in $Re$, the three data sets
   240	agree within their scatter.
   241	
   242	A least-squares fit of $C_D$ against $\log_{10} Re$ gives a slope of
   243	\CdTrend{} per decade, a small increase across the tested range
   244	comparable to the run-to-run scatter.
   245	For each cylinder, $Re$ and $Fr_D$ both scale with $U$, so this trend
   246	cannot be attributed to Reynolds number alone (section~\ref{sec:disc}).
   247	
   248	The measured values fall within the range usually quoted for subcritical
   249	two-dimensional cylinders \todo{compare quantitatively with the chosen
   250	reference data, e.g.\ at $Re = 10^4$ and $4\times10^4$}.
   251	
   252	\begin{figure}
   253	  \centering
   254	  \includegraphics{cd_vs_re.pdf}
   255	  \caption{Drag coefficient against Reynolds number. Error bars are
   256	  standard uncertainties from the force measurement only (excluding speed,
   257	  diameter and length). The open symbol is run~17, which is excluded
   258	  because of load cell drift (section~\ref{sec:quality}).}
   259	  \label{fig:cd}
   260	\end{figure}
   261	
   262	\begin{table}
   263	  \centering
   264	  \caption{Cylinder geometry, test conditions and mean drag coefficient.
   265	  $S/C$ is the ratio of the submerged frontal area to the tank
   266	  cross-section, $N$ is the number of runs used, and $s$ is the standard
   267	  deviation of $C_D$ over those runs.}
   268	  \label{tab:cylinders}
   269	  \small

   271	\end{table}

   273	%-----------------------------------------------------------------------
   274	\section{Discussion}
   275	\label{sec:disc}
   276	
   277	\paragraph{Blockage.}
   278	The frontal area of the submerged cylinder occupies
   279	$S/C = \BlockageOne$, \BlockageOneHalf{} and \BlockageTwo\% of the tank
   280	cross-section. Blockage accelerates the flow past the model and raises the
   281	measured drag. For a closed tunnel, a simple continuity estimate raises the
   282	effective velocity by $1/(1-S/C)$, which would lower the per-cylinder mean
   283	$C_D$ to \CdContOne, \CdContOneHalf{} and \CdContTwo.
   284	This estimate is probably an upper bound on the correction here, because
   285	the tank has a free surface rather than a fourth wall.
   286	\citet{WestApelt1982} found that blockage below about 6\% had only a small
   287	effect on the mean flow around a circular cylinder at similar $Re$
   288	\todo{verify this statement against the paper}.
   289	A wake-blockage method such as \citet{Maskell1963} could also be applied
   290	\todo{decide whether to correct the data, and with which method; the
   291	corrections and uncorrected values are both in processed/cd.csv}.
   292	Without a correction, the per-cylinder means do not increase with $S/C$,
   293	even though $S/C$ doubles from the smallest to the largest cylinder.
   294	This suggests that blockage is not the dominant bias, or that it is offset
   295	by another effect.
   296	
   297	\paragraph{Aspect ratio, end conditions and free surface.}
   298	The aspect ratio decreases from \AROne{} to \ARTwo{} as $D$ increases.
   299	At a free end, flow passing around the tip reduces the sectional drag
   300	nearby, so $C_D$ is expected to decrease as $L/D$ decreases
   301	\citep{WestApelt1982,Zdravkovich1997}.
   302	At the upper end, the cylinder pierces the free surface. At
   303	$Fr_D$ up to \FrMax{} the surface deforms markedly, with a bow wave in
   304	front and a depression behind, which changes both the wetted length and the
   305	near-surface pressure distribution \citep{ChaplinTeigen2003}.
   306	Increasing $D$ in this experiment increases blockage, which raises $C_D$,
   307	and decreases $L/D$, which lowers it. These two effects can partly cancel,
   308	so the agreement between cylinders does not show that either is small.
   309	For a given cylinder, $Re$ and $Fr_D$ also increase together, which is why
   310	the weak upward trend of $C_D$ with $Re$ cannot be separated from a
   311	free-surface effect.
   312	\todo{Was the free surface/waterline observed or filmed? Any visible
   313	ventilation at the highest speeds?}
   314	
   315	\paragraph{Water temperature.}
   316	The three campaigns were carried out at different water temperatures
   317	(about 17, 15 and 14\,$^\circ$C). Using the viscosity at the measured
   318	temperature, rather than a nominal 20\,$^\circ$C value, shifts the data by
   319	6--17\% in $Re$. For a relatively flat $C_D(Re)$ this barely changes the
   320	conclusions, but the correction is required for any comparison at matched
   321	$Re$.
   322	
   323	\paragraph{Recommendations for further tests.}
   324	To separate these effects, further tests could vary the submerged length at
   325	fixed $D$, which changes $L/D$ and $S/C$ independently of $Re$; repeat
   326	selected conditions to measure repeatability directly; fit an end plate to
   327	the free end; and calibrate up to at least 25~N.
   328	
   329	%-----------------------------------------------------------------------
   330	\section{Conclusions}
   331	\label{sec:conclusions}
   332	
   333	Mean drag was measured on three smooth circular cylinders towed vertically
   334	through a water tank for $Re = \ReMin$--$\ReMax$.
   335	With water properties evaluated at the measured temperature, the drag
   336	coefficient is $\CdMeanAll \pm \CdStdAll$. It shows no resolvable
   337	dependence on diameter and only a weak increase with $Re$
   338	(\CdTrend{} per decade). The values are consistent with the range reported
   339	for subcritical cylinders.
   340	Blockage (up to \BlockageTwo\%), finite aspect ratio and the free surface
   341	are each expected to bias $C_D$ by several percent. Because they tend to
   342	oppose one another and are coupled in the present test matrix, they cannot
   343	be separated with these data.
   344	A post-run zero check proved an effective way to detect a faulty run.
   345	\todo{Conclusions to be revised once the blockage-correction decision and
   346	literature comparison are made.}

    50	\section{Introduction}
    51	\label{sec:intro}
    52	
    53	The mean drag of a circular cylinder in cross-flow is among the most
    54	thoroughly documented quantities in fluid mechanics
    55	\citep{Roshko1961,Zdravkovich1997,Williamson1996}.
    56	In the subcritical regime, $10^3 \lesssim Re \lesssim 2\times10^5$, the
    57	boundary layer separates laminar, the wake is dominated by periodic vortex
    58	shedding, and the drag coefficient of a nominally two-dimensional cylinder is
    59	roughly constant at $C_D \approx 1.0$--1.2
    60	\todo{cite specific reference data and the value you want to compare
    61	against}.
    62	
    63	Laboratory measurements rarely reproduce the two-dimensional ideal.
    64	Finite span, end conditions, blockage by the facility walls and, for
    65	surface-piercing models, the free surface all modify the measured drag
    66	\citep{WestApelt1982,ChaplinTeigen2003}.
    67	Tow tanks are attractive for such measurements because the free-stream is
    68	quiescent and its velocity is set by the carriage, but the model typically
    69	pierces the free surface and spans only part of the water depth.
    70	
    71	\todo{Motivation: why these measurements? E.g., facility validation, a
    72	teaching lab benchmark, a baseline for a later study. State the contribution
    73	clearly here.}
    74	In this paper we report drag measurements on three cylinders over a
    75	tenfold range of Reynolds number, describe the calibration and data
    76	reduction in detail, and assess the main sources of bias.

   139	\section{Data reduction}
   140	\label{sec:reduction}
   141	
   142	\subsection{Mean drag force}
   143	
   144	For each run, the zero (tare) voltage is the mean over the first second,
   145	while the carriage is at rest. The force signal is
   146	$F(t) = [V(t) - V_\mathrm{tare}]/S$, where $S$ is the calibration
   147	sensitivity in force for that campaign, and the mean drag
   148	$\overline{F}$ is the average of $F(t)$ over the constant-speed window
   149	$3 < t < 8$~s (figure~\ref{fig:timeseries}a).
   150	The window starts after the start-up transient has decayed and ends before
   151	the carriage decelerates; it contains between about 4 and 43 vortex shedding
   152	cycles, depending on speed and diameter, assuming a Strouhal number of 0.2.
   153	\todo{Confirm the window against the carriage speed record if
   154	available.}
   155	
   156	\begin{figure}
   157	  \centering
   158	  \includegraphics{timeseries.pdf}
   159	  \caption{Load cell force records. (a) A typical run: shading marks the tare
   160	  window and the averaging window, and the black line is $\overline{F}$.
   161	  (b) Run~17, in which the signal drifts upward through the tow and does not
   162	  return to zero once the carriage stops; this run is excluded.}
   163	  \label{fig:timeseries}
   164	\end{figure}
   165	
   166	\subsection{Drag coefficient and Reynolds number}
   167	
   168	The drag coefficient and Reynolds number are
   169	\begin{equation}
   170	  C_D = \frac{\overline{F}}{\tfrac12 \rho U^2 D L},
   171	  \qquad
   172	  Re = \frac{U D}{\nu},
   173	\end{equation}
   174	where $U$ is the nominal carriage speed and $L$ is the submerged length.
   175	The density $\rho$ and kinematic viscosity $\nu$ are evaluated at the water
   176	temperature recorded for each run, using the correlations of
   177	\citet{Kell1975} and \citet{Kestin1978}.
   178	Water temperatures in these tests were 3--6\,$^\circ$C below 20\,$^\circ$C,
   179	so using the 20\,$^\circ$C viscosity would have overestimated $Re$ by
   180	\ReBiasMin--\ReBiasMax\%.
   181	We also report the diameter-based Froude number
   182	$Fr_D = U/\sqrt{gD}$, which ranges from \FrMin{} to \FrMax.
   183	
   184	\subsection{Data quality checks}
   185	\label{sec:quality}
   186	
   187	As a check on zero drift, the mean signal over the final second of each
   188	record, when the carriage is again at rest, is compared with the tare.
   189	For 29 of the 30 runs, this post-run zero shift is below 5~mN.
   190	For run~17 (50.8~mm cylinder, 0.8~m/s) the shift is \RunSeventeenShift~N,
   191	and the signal increases steadily throughout the tow
   192	(figure~\ref{fig:timeseries}b). This agrees with the experimenter's note
   193	at the time. Run~17 is therefore excluded. Its uncorrected drag
   194	coefficient is \RunSeventeenCd. If the zero is instead assumed to drift
   195	linearly between the pre- and post-run rest periods, $C_D$ becomes
   196	\RunSeventeenCdCorr, which agrees with the neighbouring runs. This suggests
   197	that the anomaly is instrumental, but we do not use the corrected value.
   198	\todo{Repeat run 17 if the cylinder can be re-tested; identify cause of
   199	drift (e.g.\ thermal, cable, mount slip).}
   200	
   201	The mean force in run~20 (\FMax~N) slightly exceeds the largest
   202	calibration load (\CalMaxLoad~N). Given the linearity of the calibration,
   203	we retain this run, but note that it relies on a small extrapolation.
   204	
   205	\subsection{Uncertainty}
   206	
   207	The standard uncertainty of $\overline{F}$ combines three contributions
   208	in quadrature:
   209	(i) the largest calibration residual, as a conservative bound on
   210	non-linearity and zero error;
   211	(ii) the standard error of the sensitivity fit; and
   212	(iii) the standard error of the mean over the averaging window, which
   213	treats each shedding cycle as one independent sample.
   214	The resulting standard uncertainty in $C_D$ is \UCdMin--\UCdMax\%
   215	(median \UCdMedian\%). The largest values occur at the lowest speeds,
   216	where the mean force is only a few tenths of a newton and the calibration
   217	residual dominates.
   218	These estimates exclude uncertainties in carriage speed, diameter and
   219	submerged length; a 1\% error in $U$ alone would contribute 2\% to $C_D$.
   220	\todo{Add carriage speed, $D$ and $L$ uncertainties (meniscus/waterline,
   221	free-surface set-down at higher speeds) and update the budget.}
   222	There are no repeat runs at the same condition, so run-to-run repeatability
   223	can only be inferred from the scatter of $C_D$ about its mean, which is
   224	$\pm\CdStdAll$ (one standard deviation).

   227	\section{Results}
   228	\label{sec:results}
   229	
   230	Figure~\ref{fig:cd} shows $C_D$ against $Re$ for all three cylinders, and
   231	table~\ref{tab:cylinders} summarises each data set.
   232	Over the full range $Re = \ReMin$--$\ReMax$, the drag coefficient lies
   233	between about 1.09 and 1.22, with an overall mean of
   234	$\CdMeanAll \pm \CdStdAll$.
   235	The per-cylinder means are \CdMeanOne{} ($D = 25.4$~mm),
   236	\CdMeanOneHalf{} (38.1~mm) and \CdMeanTwo{} (50.8~mm). These differ by
   237	less than the scatter within each set, so diameter has no resolvable
   238	effect.
   239	In the regions where the cylinders overlap in $Re$, the three data sets
   240	agree within their scatter.
   241	
   242	A least-squares fit of $C_D$ against $\log_{10} Re$ gives a slope of
   243	\CdTrend{} per decade, a small increase across the tested range
   244	comparable to the run-to-run scatter.
   245	For each cylinder, $Re$ and $Fr_D$ both scale with $U$, so this trend
   246	cannot be attributed to Reynolds number alone (section~\ref{sec:disc}).
   247

   274	\section{Discussion}
   275	\label{sec:disc}
   276	
   277	\paragraph{Blockage.}
   278	The frontal area of the submerged cylinder occupies
   279	$S/C = \BlockageOne$, \BlockageOneHalf{} and \BlockageTwo\% of the tank
   280	cross-section. Blockage accelerates the flow past the model and raises the
   281	measured drag. For a closed tunnel, a simple continuity estimate raises the
   282	effective velocity by $1/(1-S/C)$, which would lower the per-cylinder mean
   283	$C_D$ to \CdContOne, \CdContOneHalf{} and \CdContTwo.
   284	This estimate is probably an upper bound on the correction here, because
   285	the tank has a free surface rather than a fourth wall.
   286	\citet{WestApelt1982} found that blockage below about 6\% had only a small
   287	effect on the mean flow around a circular cylinder at similar $Re$
   288	\todo{verify this statement against the paper}.
   289	A wake-blockage method such as \citet{Maskell1963} could also be applied
   290	\todo{decide whether to correct the data, and with which method; the
   291	corrections and uncorrected values are both in processed/cd.csv}.
   292	Without a correction, the per-cylinder means do not increase with $S/C$,
   293	even though $S/C$ doubles from the smallest to the largest cylinder.
   294	This suggests that blockage is not the dominant bias, or that it is offset
   295	by another effect.
   296	
   297	\paragraph{Aspect ratio, end conditions and free surface.}
   298	The aspect ratio decreases from \AROne{} to \ARTwo{} as $D$ increases.
   299	At a free end, flow passing around the tip reduces the sectional drag
   300	nearby, so $C_D$ is expected to decrease as $L/D$ decreases
   301	\citep{WestApelt1982,Zdravkovich1997}.
   302	At the upper end, the cylinder pierces the free surface. At
   303	$Fr_D$ up to \FrMax{} the surface deforms markedly, with a bow wave in
   304	front and a depression behind, which changes both the wetted length and the
   305	near-surface pressure distribution \citep{ChaplinTeigen2003}.
   306	Increasing $D$ in this experiment increases blockage, which raises $C_D$,
   307	and decreases $L/D$, which lowers it. These two effects can partly cancel,
   308	so the agreement between cylinders does not show that either is small.
   309	For a given cylinder, $Re$ and $Fr_D$ also increase together, which is why
   310	the weak upward trend of $C_D$ with $Re$ cannot be separated from a
   311	free-surface effect.
   312	\todo{Was the free surface/waterline observed or filmed? Any visible
   313	ventilation at the highest speeds?}
   314	
   315	\paragraph{Water temperature.}
   316	The three campaigns were carried out at different water temperatures
   317	(about 17, 15 and 14\,$^\circ$C). Using the viscosity at the measured
   318	temperature, rather than a nominal 20\,$^\circ$C value, shifts the data by
   319	6--17\% in $Re$. For a relatively flat $C_D(Re)$ this barely changes the
   320	conclusions, but the correction is required for any comparison at matched
   321	$Re$.
   322	
   323	\paragraph{Recommendations for further tests.}
   324	To separate these effects, further tests could vary the submerged length at
   325	fixed $D$, which changes $L/D$ and $S/C$ independently of $Re$; repeat
   326	selected conditions to measure repeatability directly; fit an end plate to
   327	the free end; and calibrate up to at least 25~N.

   330	\section{Conclusions}
   331	\label{sec:conclusions}
   332	
   333	Mean drag was measured on three smooth circular cylinders towed vertically
   334	through a water tank for $Re = \ReMin$--$\ReMax$.
   335	With water properties evaluated at the measured temperature, the drag
   336	coefficient is $\CdMeanAll \pm \CdStdAll$. It shows no resolvable
   337	dependence on diameter and only a weak increase with $Re$
   338	(\CdTrend{} per decade). The values are consistent with the range reported
   339	for subcritical cylinders.
   340	Blockage (up to \BlockageTwo\%), finite aspect ratio and the free surface
   341	are each expected to bias $C_D$ by several percent. Because they tend to
   342	oppose one another and are coupled in the present test matrix, they cannot
   343	be separated with these data.
   344	A post-run zero check proved an effective way to detect a faulty run.

How the current draft covers each comment:

**Reviewer 1.1 (viscosity at 20 °C).** Already fixed. `scripts/calc_cd.py` works out ρ and ν from each run's logged temperature (Kell 1975 and Kestin et al. 1978, in `scripts/towtank.py`). The paper says this in the abstract (line 31), §3.2 (lines 175–180) and the "Water temperature" paragraph of the Discussion. It also gives the size of the error: using 20 °C would have overstated Re by 6–17%. I spot-checked the viscosities against standard values for 13.7–17.6 °C and they're right.

**Reviewer 1.2 (run 17).** Already excluded, and the paper says so. Its post-run zero shift is 4.2 N. Every other run is under 3.5 mN, against a 50 mN threshold. Run 17 is discussed in §3.3 (lines 190–197) and shown in Fig. 2b. It appears as an open symbol in Fig. 3 and is footnoted in the run table. The paper also gives its corrected value (C_D 1.36 → 1.16 if you assume linear drift) but doesn't use it. Without run 17, the 2 in. mean is 1.16, compared with 1.18 in the old notebook.

> **R1.1** We thank the reviewer. Re is now computed with ρ and ν evaluated at the measured water temperature of each run (13.7–17.6 °C) using the Kell (1975) and Kestin et al. >
> **R2.1** The abstract now states the Reynolds number range, Re = 4,700–49,800.

The "now" wording assumes the reviewers really did see the older version. Check that before sending.

If you want to go beyond the comments, one possible follow-up: the Discussion hardcodes "6--17%" (line 319) and the Results hardcode "1.09 and 1.22" (line 233).
